results.q: What happens when an RTU frame has a bad CRC?
answer: Invalid data is caught in _modbus_rtu_check_integrity() (src/modbus-rtu.c:387): it checks `crc_calculated != crc_received`, and when that is true it checks `ctx->error_recovery & MODBUS_ERROR_RECOVERY_PROTOCOL` (MODBUS_ERROR_RECOVERY_PROTOCOL = 4) (line 395); if true it calls _modbus_rtu_flush(); then it sets `errno = EMBBADCRC` (line 398); then it returns `-1` (line 399), so the rest of _modbus_rtu_check_integrity() is skipped.

Consequence: main() checks `errno == EMBBADCRC` (tests/unit-test-server.c:149); `errno == EMBBADCRC` depends on runtime values, so it may call close() and may call __darwin_fd_clr() and may call modbus_read_registers() and may call malloc() and may call memset().

Consequence: _modbus_tcp_select() checks `errno == EINTR` (src/modbus-tcp.c:887); `errno == EINTR` depends on runtime values, so it may return early and may call __builtin_bzero and may call __darwin_fd_set().

_modbus_rtu_flush() sets `modbus_rtu_t *ctx_rtu = ctx->backend_data` (line 1211); then it sets `ctx_rtu->w_ser.n_bytes = 0` (line 1212); then it calls PurgeComm() (line 1213); then it returns `(PurgeComm(ctx_rtu->w_ser.fd, PURGE_RXCLEAR) == FALSE)` (line 1213).

Consequence: win32_ser_select() checks `ReadFile(ws->fd, &ws->buf, max_len, &ws->n_bytes, NULL)` (src/modbus-rtu.c:208); `ReadFile(ws->fd, &ws->buf, max_len, &ws->n_bytes, NULL)` depends on runtime values, so it may return early.
It is computed in crc16():
crc16() (src/modbus-rtu.c:119).

Step by step, it sets `uint8_t crc_hi = 0xFF` (line 121); then it sets `uint8_t crc_lo = 0xFF` (line 122); then it repeats while `buffer_length--` (line 126); then it sets `i = crc_lo ^ *buffer++` (line 127); then it sets `crc_lo = crc_hi ^ table_crc_hi[i]` (line 128); then it sets `crc_hi = table_crc_lo[i]` (line 129); then it returns `(crc_hi << 8 | crc_lo)` (line 132).
The result is stored in _modbus_rtu_send_msg_pre.crc by _modbus_rtu_send_msg_pre() (src/modbus-rtu.c:143: `uint16_t crc = crc16(req, req_length)`).
The result is stored in _modbus_rtu_check_integrity.crc_calculated by _modbus_rtu_check_integrity() (src/modbus-rtu.c:383: `crc_calculated = crc16(msg, msg_length - 2)`).

It is called by _modbus_rtu_send_msg_pre() at src/modbus-rtu.c:143 with (`req`, `req_length`); _modbus_rtu_check_integrity() at src/modbus-rtu.c:383 with (`msg`, `msg_length - 2`). The full chain from the program's start is: main() → modbus_write_and_read_registers() → send_msg() → _modbus_rtu_send_msg_pre() → crc16().

It is called by _modbus_receive_msg() (through the dispatch table _modbus_backend.check_integrity) at src/modbus.c:546 (_modbus_rtu_check_integrity() is listed in the table _modbus_rtu_backend at src/modbus-rtu.c:1286) with (`ctx`, `msg`, `msg_length`) — `int msg_length = 0` (line 372), only when `!ctx->backend->is_connected(ctx)` is false, only when `ctx->s < 0 || ctx->s >= FD_SETSIZE` is false. The full chain from the program's start is: main() → modbus_write_and_read_registers() → _modbus_receive_msg() → _modbus_rtu_check_integrity().

results.q: What happens when the slave does not answer before the response timeout?
answer: Losing the data is detected in _connect() (src/modbus-tcp.c:319), which checks `rc == 0`.
When that happens it sets `errno = ETIMEDOUT`; returns.
_connect() also stops early when `rc == 0 && optval == 0` (line 327) — so without fresh valid data it does not reach those calls either.
Its caller _modbus_tcp_pi_connect() checks `rc == -1` (src/modbus-tcp.c:494) and then calls closesocket().

results.q: What does modbus_new_rtu do when the baud rate is not positive?
answer: modbus_new_rtu() (src/modbus-rtu.c:1298) — clang-format on.

Step by step, it checks `device == NULL || *device == 0` (line 1305); if true it calls fprintf() and sets `errno = EINVAL` and returns `NULL` straight away; then it checks `baud <= 0` (line 1312); if true it calls fprintf() and sets `errno = EINVAL` and returns `NULL` straight away; then it checks `data_bit < 5 || data_bit > 8` (line 1319); if true it calls fprintf() and sets `errno = EINVAL` and returns `NULL` straight away; then it checks `stop_bit != 1 && stop_bit != 2` (line 1326); if true it calls fprintf() and sets `errno = EINVAL` and returns `NULL` straight away; then it calls malloc() and stores the result in `ctx` (line 1332); then it checks `ctx == NULL` (line 1333); if true it returns `NULL` straight away; then it calls _modbus_init_common() (line 1337); then it sets `ctx->backend = &_modbus_rtu_backend` (line 1338); then it calls malloc() and stores the result in `ctx->backend_data` (line 1339); then it checks `ctx->backend_data == NULL` (line 1340); if true it calls modbus_free() and sets `errno = ENOMEM` and returns `NULL` straight away; ….

It is called by main() at tests/bandwidth-client.c:76, only when `use_backend == TCP` is false (TCP = 0); main() at tests/bandwidth-server-one.c:56, only when `use_backend == TCP` is false (TCP = 0); main() at tests/unit-test-client.c:125, only when `use_backend == TCP` is false (TCP = 0), only when `use_backend == TCP_PI` is false (TCP_PI = 1); main() at tests/unit-test-client.c:793, only when `ctx == NULL` is false, only when `modbus_connect(ctx) == -1` is false, only when `test_server(ctx, use_backend) == -1` is false. The full chain from the program's start is: main() → modbus_new_rtu().

The values it updates are used later by send_msg() (uses _modbus.backend, errno); _modbus_receive_msg() (uses _modbus.backend, errno); modbus_proxy() (uses _modbus.backend, errno); _modbus_rtu_send() (uses _modbus.backend_data, win32_ser.fd).

results.q: Where is the slave address stored?
answer: It is written here: `ctx->slave = slave` in _modbus_set_slave() (src/modbus-rtu.c:84); `ctx->slave = slave` in _modbus_set_slave() (src/modbus-tcp.c:93); `ctx->slave = slave` in _modbus_set_slave() (src/modbus-tcp.c:97); `ctx->slave = -1` in _modbus_init_common() (src/modbus.c:1982); `ctx->slave = MODBUS_TCP_SLAVE` in modbus_new_tcp() (src/modbus-tcp.c:1009); `ctx->slave = MODBUS_TCP_SLAVE` in modbus_new_tcp_pi() (src/modbus-tcp.c:1059).

results.q: What happens when a request asks for an illegal data address?
answer: Invalid data is caught in modbus_reply() (src/modbus.c:903): it checks `mapping_address < 0 || (mapping_address + nb) > nb_bits`, and when that is true it calls response_exception(ctx, &sft, MODBUS_EXCEPTION_ILLEGAL_DATA_ADDRESS, rsp, FALSE, …).

When it does not return there, modbus_reply() goes on to call response_exception() with (`ctx`, `&sft`, `MODBUS_EXCEPTION_ILLEGAL_DATA_ADDRESS`) (line 945); response_exception() with (`ctx`, `&sft`, `MODBUS_EXCEPTION_ILLEGAL_DATA_ADDRESS`) (line 968); response_exception() with (`ctx`, `&sft`, `MODBUS_EXCEPTION_ILLEGAL_DATA_VALUE`) (line 982); response_exception() with (`ctx`, `&sft`, `MODBUS_EXCEPTION_ILLEGAL_DATA_VALUE`) (line 1004); response_exception() with (`ctx`, `&sft`, `MODBUS_EXCEPTION_ILLEGAL_DATA_ADDRESS`) (line 1020).

response_exception() checks `ctx->debug` (line 774); if true it calls __builtin_va_start(), vfprintf(), __builtin_va_end(); then it checks `to_flush` (line 783); if true it calls _sleep_response_timeout(), modbus_flush(); then it sets `sft->function = sft->function + 0x80` (line 789); then it calls one of _modbus_rtu_build_response_basis(), _modbus_tcp_build_response_basis() through _modbus_backend.build_response_basis — which one depends on the data at run time (line 790); then it sets `rsp[rsp_length++] = exception_code` (line 791); then it returns `rsp_length` (line 793).
modbus_read_registers() (src/modbus.c:1596) — Reads the holding registers of remote device and put the data into an array.

Step by step, it checks `ctx == NULL || dest == NULL` (line 1600); if true it sets `errno = EINVAL`; if true it returns `-1` straight away; then it checks `nb < 1 || nb > MODBUS_MAX_READ_REGISTERS` (MODBUS_MAX_READ_REGISTERS = 125) (line 1605); if true it calls fprintf() and sets `errno = EMBXILVAL` and returns `-1` straight away; then it calls read_registers() and stores the result in `status` (line 1616); then it returns `status` (line 1617).

It is called by main() at tests/bandwidth-client.c:135, only when `modbus_connect(ctx) == -1` is false, repeatedly inside `for (i = 0; i < n_loop; i++)`; main() at tests/proxy-test-client.c:233, only when `ctx == NULL` is false, only when `modbus_connect(ctx) == -1` is false; main() at tests/random-test-client.c:152, repeatedly inside `while (nb_loop++ < LOOP)`, repeatedly inside `for (addr = ADDRESS_START; addr < ADDRESS_END; addr++)`, only when `rc != 1` is false; main() at tests/random-test-client.c:178, repeatedly inside `while (nb_loop++ < LOOP)`, repeatedly inside `for (addr = ADDRESS_START; addr < ADDRESS_END; addr++)`, only when `rc != nb` is false. The full chain from the program's start is: main() → modbus_read_registers().
The values it updates are used later by _modbus_tcp_select() (uses errno); _error_print() (uses errno); send_msg() (uses errno); _modbus_receive_msg() (uses errno).

results.q: What does modbus_read_registers return when too many registers are requested?
answer: This is handled in modbus_read_registers() (src/modbus.c:1605): it checks `nb < 1 || nb > MODBUS_MAX_READ_REGISTERS`, and when that is true it records it (`errno = EMBXILVAL`) and returns `-1`, so the rest of modbus_read_registers() is skipped.
Because it returns early, these do not happen in this case: read_registers() — the previous values stay in place.

Consequence: main() checks `errno == EMBBADCRC` (tests/unit-test-server.c:149); `errno == EMBBADCRC` depends on runtime values, so it may call close() and may call __darwin_fd_clr() and may call modbus_read_registers() and may call malloc() and may call memset().

Consequence: _modbus_tcp_select() checks `errno == EINTR` (src/modbus-tcp.c:887); `errno == EINTR` depends on runtime values, so it may return early and may call __builtin_bzero and may call __darwin_fd_set().
Bad input is also rejected in other places: read_registers() drops it when `nb > MODBUS_MAX_READ_REGISTERS` (src/modbus.c:1557), counting it in errno.

results.q: Where is the response timeout set?
answer: It is set in modbus_set_response_timeout():
modbus_set_response_timeout() (src/modbus.c:2067).

Step by step, it checks `ctx == NULL || (to_sec == 0 && to_usec == 0) || to_usec > 999999` (line 2069); if true it sets `errno = EINVAL`; if true it returns `-1` straight away; then it sets `ctx->response_timeout.tv_sec = to_sec` (line 2074); then it sets `ctx->response_timeout.tv_usec = to_usec` (line 2075); then it returns `0` (line 2076).
The update itself: `ctx->response_timeout.tv_sec = to_sec` (src/modbus.c:2074); `ctx->response_timeout.tv_usec = to_usec` (src/modbus.c:2075).

Related values are also set here: `ctx->response_timeout.tv_sec = 0` in _modbus_init_common() (src/modbus.c:1989); `ctx->response_timeout.tv_usec = _RESPONSE_TIMEOUT` in _modbus_init_common() (src/modbus.c:1990); `ctx->byte_timeout.tv_sec = to_sec` in modbus_set_byte_timeout() (src/modbus.c:2100); `ctx->byte_timeout.tv_usec = to_usec` in modbus_set_byte_timeout() (src/modbus.c:2101); `ctx->indication_timeout.tv_sec = to_sec` in modbus_set_indication_timeout() (src/modbus.c:2127); `ctx->indication_timeout.tv_usec = to_usec` in modbus_set_indication_timeout() (src/modbus.c:2128).

results.q: How is a request sent over the serial line?
answer: This is done by _modbus_rtu_send() (src/modbus-rtu.c:266): it calls WriteFile() (Win32 file/serial write) at src/modbus-rtu.c:271.
_modbus_rtu_send() (src/modbus-rtu.c:266).

Step by step, it sets `modbus_rtu_t *ctx_rtu = ctx->backend_data` (line 269); then it checks `(WriteFile(ctx_rtu->w_ser.fd, req, req_length, &n_bytes, NULL))` (line 271); then it returns `(WriteFile(ctx_rtu->w_ser.fd, req, req_length, &n_bytes, NULL))` (line 271).
_modbus_backend.select is a field of type `int (*)(modbus_t *, fd_set *, struct timeval *, int)`, defined in src/modbus-private.h:92.
Nothing in this code assigns _modbus_backend.select after its declaration.
It is read by _modbus_receive_msg() (line 429).
_modbus_backend.select holds a function: at run time it points to _modbus_rtu_select(), _modbus_tcp_select(); it is called by _modbus_receive_msg().
In short: _modbus_backend.select carries a value and consumed by _modbus_receive_msg().

There is no `modbus_reset_crc_table` in this code (none of its 1267 indexed symbols has that name). The closest names are table_crc_hi (src/modbus-rtu.c:33), table_crc_lo (src/modbus-rtu.c:55), crc16() (src/modbus-rtu.c:119), described below.
table_crc_hi is a global variable of type `const uint8_t[256]`, defined in src/modbus-rtu.c:33 — the code describes it as: "Table of CRC values for high-order byte".
Nothing in this code assigns table_crc_hi after its declaration.
It is read by crc16() (line 128).
Following where its value goes: table_crc_hi → crc16() → _modbus_rtu_check_integrity() → fprintf() — so it ultimately influences fprintf(), which is an output (file/console log).
In short: table_crc_hi carries a value and consumed by crc16(), feeding fprintf().
